questions.q: What is the main advantage of the Microsoft Graph Security API's unified alert and incident schema, per this lesson?
options: It eliminates the need for any authentication when querying alerts
It automatically takes containment action on every alert without a human in the loop
It returns alerts and incidents from multiple Defender products and Sentinel in one normalized schema, instead of five different product-specific shapes
It only works with Microsoft Sentinel and not with Defender XDR
questions.explain: The Graph Security API normalizes alerts and incidents across Defender for Endpoint, Identity, Office 365, Cloud Apps, and Sentinel into one consistent schema, so you write one parser instead of several.

questions.q: Which Graph Security API resource represents one or more correlated alerts grouped into a single case?
options: /security/incidents
/security/alerts_v2
/security/secureScores
/security/tiIndicators
questions.explain: /security/incidents groups one or more correlated alerts into a single incident, with its own severity, status, determination, and assigned owner.

questions.q: In the client-credentials flow with MSAL shown in this lesson, why is the scope always requested as "https://graph.microsoft.com/.default"?
options: Because .default disables all application permissions
Because it tells Azure AD to issue a token covering whatever application permissions were already granted and consented, rather than listing individual Graph scopes
Because .default is required only for delegated, user-signed-in flows
Because it forces the token to expire immediately after use
questions.explain: For app-only authentication, requesting the .default scope tells Azure AD to issue a token for the application permissions already granted with admin consent.

questions.q: What does the @odata.nextLink field in a Graph API response indicate?
options: The severity level of the next alert in the response
An error code that must be handled before continuing
The Azure AD tenant ID the alert belongs to
A cursor URL to fetch the next page of results; its absence means there are no more pages
questions.explain: Graph paginates results, and @odata.nextLink is the cursor telling a script whether more pages exist. A pagination loop keeps following it until it's missing from the response.

questions.q: How does the extract_ips() pattern in this lesson identify which evidence entries contain IP addresses?
options: It checks each evidence entry's @odata.type field for one ending in "ipEvidence"
It assumes the first entry in the evidence array is always an IP address
It calls a separate /security/ipAddresses endpoint
It parses the alert's title text looking for IP-formatted strings
questions.explain: Each evidence entry carries an @odata.type discriminator; the function loops through evidence and checks for entries whose type ends in "ipEvidence" before collecting the ipAddress field.
